[approach_variants] That road and the campground are seasonal and open on the snowpack, not on a date.

[approach_variants] The trail follows the Inter Fork of the White River on an old mining road grade, 3.5 miles to Glacier Basin Campground (~5,935 ft): six designated sites, a toilet and a bear-proof food cache.

[approach_variants] Above Glacier Basin a climbers' path continues about a mile up the lateral moraine — conspicuously yellowish once it melts out — to the toe of the Inter Glacier at roughly 7,000 ft.
[approach_variants] The Inter Glacier is about 1,500 ft of moderate snow;
[approach_variants] it is the mildest glacier on the route but it opens real crevasses as the season goes on, and roped travel is standard.

[approach_variants] From Camp Curtis the route drops slightly and traverses onto the lower Emmons Glacier, rounding the southern side of Steamboat Prow to Camp Schurman (about 9,460 ft), where the Emmons and Winthrop glaciers split around the Prow.
[approach_variants] tent platforms are dug into snow on the Emmons side.
[approach_variants] The same Rainier permit structure applies: a per-person climbing permit for glacier travel or ground above roughly 10,000 ft, plus a wilderness permit for each overnight..
[approach_variants] Late spring through August, once the White River road and campground are open and before summer melt opens the upper crevasse fields.

name: Fuhrer Finger
text: [seasonal_hazards] Hidden crevasses on the Wilson/Nisqually approach, plus a bergschrund near the top of the finger
[approach_variants] Paradise, Glacier Vista and the Nisqually crossing to a Wilson Glacier camp.
[approach_variants] From Paradise (5,400 ft) take the paved Skyline Trail about a mile to the Glacier Vista overlook (~6,300 ft).
[approach_variants] This is where the route leaves the tourist ground: a climbers' path drops several hundred feet west off the moraine onto the Nisqually Glacier, crossing at roughly 6,200 ft.
[approach_variants] Most parties rope up before stepping onto the ice — the crossing threads crevassed terrain under an icefall and is genuinely committing in poor visibility.
[approach_variants] On the far side, a boulder-filled gully angles up and right onto the left-hand side of the Wilson Glacier.

[approach_variants] The more usual choice is to continue onto the Wapowety Cleaver and follow its crest to a high camp at roughly 9,000–9,200 ft at the edge of the Wilson Glacier, where there are rock windbreaks and a large rock buttress for shelter.
[approach_variants] The traverse of the Wilson Glacier under the Wilson Headwall to the foot of the couloir has real route-finding, and you will be doing it in the dark.
[approach_variants] Spring, while the couloir is snow-filled and the rock above is still frozen.
[approach_variants] Crevasses and icefall exposure on the Nisqually Glacier crossing at about 6,200 ft.
[approach_variants] Route-finding on the Wilson Glacier traverse, normally done in the dark.
[approach_variants] Large crevasses on the upper slopes that can force long end-runs late in the season.

[approach_variants] Positive test: from the base, you should be looking up roughly 2,000–3,000 ft of continuous snow at about 40 degrees, wide at the bottom, narrowing to an hourglass, and widening again.
[approach_variants] It runs out onto the west side of the upper Nisqually Glacier and eventually joins the upper Kautz Glacier ground near 13,000 ft.

name: Fuhrer Thumb
text: [approach_variants] Paradise, the Nisqually crossing and the Wilson Glacier to the narrow couloir.

[approach_variants] From Paradise, take the Skyline Trail to Glacier Vista and drop west down the Nisqually Moraine onto the Nisqually Glacier, cross it westward, then work up the Wilson Gully, the Wilson Bench and the Wilson Chute on the west side of the glacier toward the camps

[approach_variants] From left to right the three features are: the Wilson Glacier headwall, the Fuhrer Thumb, the Fuhrer Finger.

[approach_variants] Learn that order before you leave the car — it is the only thing separating this route from its two neighbours in the dark, and all three start within a short distance of each other off the same bench of glacier.

[approach_variants] If you are looking at an open face rather than into a gully at all, you have gone one too far left and you are under the Wilson Glacier Headwall, which is a harder proposition than either couloir.
[approach_variants] What being too early in the approach looks like: if you have not crossed the Nisqually Glacier westward, you have not started.
[approach_variants] Everything about this route is on the west side of that glacier, under The Castle and the Kautz Ice Cliff.

[overview] A narrower, steeper variation of the Fuhrer Finger, climbing the couloir immediately to its west before rejoining the Finger route on the west side of the Nisqually Glacier at about 11,500'.

name: Gibraltar Ledges
text: [approach_variants] Paradise (5,420 ft) to Camp Muir (10,080 ft) by the Skyline Trail and the Muir Snowfield, the same carry as the Disappointment Cleaver.

[approach_variants] Not east across the Cowlitz Glacier: east is Cathedral Gap and the Disappointment Cleaver, the opposite side of camp.

[approach_variants] At the base of Gib Rock you should find an exposed shelf of snow and rock that traverses horizontally along the rock's southwest-facing base for about a third of a mile.

[approach_variants] The ledges deliver you to the foot of the Gibraltar Chute, and the chute is joined at roughly 12,300 ft and climbed for about 400 ft of 45-degree snow to the top of Gibraltar Rock.
[approach_variants] Above that, most parties trend onto the upper Ingraham for another 1,200 ft to avoid crevasses and join the standard route near 13,800 ft.

[overview] From Camp Muir the route ascends the western edge of the Cowlitz Glacier below the Cowlitz Cleaver, passes beneath a rock feature called the Beehive, and crosses the cleaver through a notch to reach the base of Gibraltar Rock.

[overview] From about 11,800 ft the route follows exposed snow-and-rock 'ledges' along the base of Gibraltar Rock for roughly a third of a mile to the top of Gibraltar Chute (~12,600 ft, sometimes called 'Camp Comfort');
